'''Spencer Ferguson Silver III''' (February 6, 1941{{snd}}May 8, 2021) was an American chemist and inventor who specialized in adhesives. [[3M]] credits him with having devised the adhesive that [[Arthur Fry]] used to create [[Post-it Note]]s.<ref name="3M">{{cite web|title =About Post-it Brand |publisher=3M| url =http://www.post-it.com/wps/portal/3M/en_US/Post_It/Global/Home/About/About/ |access-date =January 8, 2011}}</ref><ref name="NIHF"/>

== Early life ==
Spencer Ferguson Silver III was born in [[San Antonio, Texas]], on February 6, 1941, to Bernice (née Wendt) and Spencer Silver Jr.<ref name="NIHF">{{cite web |title=Inductees > Spencer Silver |url=https://www.invent.org/inductees/spencer-silver |website=National Inventors Hall of Fame |publisher=NIHF |access-date= November 11, 2019}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> His father was an accountant while his mother was a secretary.<ref name=":0" /> He majored in chemistry at [[Arizona State University]], earning a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in 1962, then earned a doctorate in [[organic chemistry]] from the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]] in 1966, before taking a position as a Senior Chemist in 3M's Central Research Labs.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Spencer F. Silver|url=https://www.msthalloffame.org/spencer_silver.htm|access-date=May 13, 2021|website=www.msthalloffame.org}}</ref>

== Career ==
Silver started his career at [[3M]]'s central research laboratory as a senior chemist focused on developing pressure sensitive adhesives.<ref name=":0" /> He started working in 1968 on trying to create a strong adhesive that could be used for aircraft construction.<ref name=":0" /> However, he failed in that objective and ended up developing a "low-tack" adhesive made of tiny [[wikt:acrylic|acrylic]] spheres that would stick only where they were tangent to a given surface, rather than flat up against it. The adhesive's grip was strong enough to hold papers together, but weak enough to allow the papers to be pulled apart again without being torn. It could also be used again and again. The adhesive, acrylate copolymer microspheres, was patented in 1972 and described as suitable for use as a spray.<ref>{{cite web |title=US Patent 3691140A Acrylate copolymer microspheres |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US3691140A/en |website=Google Patents |publisher=Google Inc |access-date=October 24, 2019}}</ref>

In 1974, [[Arthur Fry]], a chemical engineer in the tape division at 3M, attended an internal seminar held by Silver, who was promoting his adhesive's properties. Fry regarded it as a potential solution to a practical challenge, that of preventing paper bookmarks from falling out of his hymnal when he sang in church. Fry developed bookmarks using Silver's adhesive, preventing them from leaving residue, and sought to interest others within the 3M company in them.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Meyer |first1=Nancy |title=Arthur Fry, Inventor of 3M's Post-it Note |url=https://wementor.com/2018/10/01/arthur-fry-inventor-of-3ms-post-it-note-part-i/ |website=WeMentor |publisher=WeMentor Inc |access-date=October 24, 2019 |date=October 1, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Flavell-While |first1=Claudia |title=Spencer Silver and Arthur Fry: the chemist and the tinkerer who created the Post-it Note |url=https://www.thechemicalengineer.com/features/cewctw-spencer-silver-and-arthur-fry-in-search-of-an-application/ |website=The Chemical Engineer |publisher=Institution of Chemical Engineers |access-date=October 25, 2019 |date=August 15, 2012}}</ref> The adhesive notes were initially marketed under the name Post 'n Peel in four cities from 1977 and as Post-it Notes from 1980 throughout the United States.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Duguid |first1=Sarah |title=First Person: 'We invented the Post-it Note' |url=https://www.ft.com/content/f08e8a9a-fcd7-11df-ae2d-00144feab49a |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/FkfOX |archive-date=December 11, 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |website=Financial Times |publisher=The Financial Times Ltd |date=December 3, 2010|access-date= November 24, 2019}}</ref> [[Post-it Note|Post-it]] as we know it was patented by Fry in 1993 as a "repositionable pressure-sensitive adhesive sheet material".<ref name=":0" />   

Silver worked for over 30 years at 3M rising to a position of a corporate scientist before retiring in 1996.<ref name=":0" /> Some of the other products that he worked on included [[Block copolymer|block copolymers]] and [[immunodiagnostics]].<ref name=":0" /> He is named in over 20 U.S. patents.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Art Fry & Spencer Silver {{!}} Lemelson|url=https://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/art-fry-spencer-silver|access-date=May 14, 2021|website=lemelson.mit.edu}}</ref> 

Silver received several awards for his work, including the 1998 [[American Chemical Society]] Award for Creative Invention<ref>{{cite web |title=ACS Award for Creative Invention |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-for-creative-invention.html |website=ACS |publisher=American Chemical Society |access-date=October 25, 2019}}</ref> and induction into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]] in 2011.<ref name="NIHF"/>  A book of Post-it notes is held in the design collection of the [[List of works in the Museum of Modern Art#Department of Architecture and Design|Museum of Modern Art]] (MoMA) in New York City, and both Silver and Fry are credited as the artists.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.moma.org/artists/23346?=undefined&page=&direction=|title = Spencer Silver &#124; MoMA}}</ref>

In 2025, the Post-it Note was included in ''[[Pirouette: Turning Points in Design]],'' an exhibition at the MoMA featuring "widely recognized design icons [...] highlighting pivotal moments in design history."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pirouette: Turning Points in Design |url=https://www.moma.org/calendar/exhibitions/5756 |access-date=2 August 2025 |website=[[The Museum of Modern Art]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=23 January 2025 |title=NASA Worm as Art, Museum of Modern Art Opens Exhibition Featuring NASA Worm |url=https://www.nasa.gov/get-involved/art-program/museum-of-modern-art-exhibits-nasa-worm/ |access-date=2 August 2025 |website=[[NASA]]}}</ref><ref name="Feeney-2025">{{Cite web |last=Feeney |first=Mark |author-link=Mark Feeney |date=23 July 2025 |title=At MoMA, designs for living |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2025/07/23/arts/moma-designs-living/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250724091754/https://www.bostonglobe.com/2025/07/23/arts/moma-designs-living/ |archive-date=24 Jul 2025 |access-date=2 August 2025 |website=[[The Boston Globe]]}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
In 1965 Silver married Linda Martin, a computer programmer whom he met when she was an undergraduate working part time at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]]'s chemistry department and he was pursuing his PhD at the same university. The couple went on to have two daughters, one of whom predeceased Silver in 2017.<ref name=":0" />

Silver was a painter who pursued art seriously after his retirement, working on oils and pastels on canvas and acrylics to create abstract paintings.<ref name=":0" />

Silver received a heart transplant in 1994. He died at his home in [[St. Paul, Minnesota]], on May 8, 2021, from [[ventricular tachycardia]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|last=Sandomir|first=Richard|date=May 13, 2021|title=Spencer Silver, an Inventor of Post-it Notes, Is Dead at 80|language=en-US|volume=170|page=A29|work=The New York Times|issue=59060|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/05/13/business/spencer-silver-dead.html|access-date=May 14, 2021|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He was 80 years old.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Painter |first1=Kristen Leigh |title=Co-inventor of Post-its, retired 3M scientist Spencer Silver, dies at 80 |url=https://m.startribune.com/co-inventor-of-post-its-retired-3m-scientist-spencer-silver-dies-at-80/600056840/ |website=Star Tribune |access-date=May 14, 2021 |language=en |date=May 13, 2021}}</ref>
